cards.explanation: The reason is that the LORD's loving devotion toward us is great. The writer says, “For great is His loving devotion toward us…” (Psalm 117:2). He doesn't hand the nations a long list. He points at who the LORD is, and that's plenty.
The answer is False. The text says the faithfulness of the LORD “endures forever.” (Psalm 117:2). No season gets mentioned at all. Forever is the only length the writer gives.
The reason is that He is good. Psalm 118 begins, “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good…” The reason is simple and short. He is good, and that's enough to start a whole psalm, friends.

The third group is those who fear the LORD. The psalm says, “Let those who fear the LORD say…” (Psalm 118:4). First comes Israel, then the house of Aaron, then those who fear the LORD. Same line each time, and a new group saying it.

The answer is True. The writer says, “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free.” (Psalm 118:5). He called and the LORD answered. Then he was set free, and I love how plain that is, friends.

It means that with the LORD on his side, people can't scare him. He says, “The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid.” Then he asks, “What can man do to me?” It's a question with a confident answer built in, the way you'd ask it when you already know.

The word is triumph. The writer says, “Therefore I will look in triumph on those who hate me.” (Psalm 118:7). The word "therefore" ties it to what came before. The LORD is his helper, so he can look at them in triumph, friends.

The answer is the LORD. “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man.” (Psalm 118:8). The next verse says it again about princes: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.” (Psalm 118:9). Same refuge both times, and it's the LORD.
The answer is True. The writer says, “All the nations surrounded me, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off.” (Psalm 118:10). Notice whose name he does it in, friends. It's the name of the LORD.

The nations were extinguished like burning thorns. The writer says, “They swarmed around me like bees, but they were extinguished like burning thorns…” (Psalm 118:12). The swarm gets loud and then it goes out. He says again that he cut them off in the name of the LORD.

The answer is False. The writer says, “I was pushed so hard I was falling, but the LORD helped me.” (Psalm 118:13). Nobody does it alone here. I know a little something about being stuck, friends, and help makes all the difference.

The answer is True. The writer says, “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.” (Psalm 118:14). Strength, song and salvation all come in one verse. That's a full cookie box of a line, bakers.

The right hand of the LORD is what performs with valor. The tents shout, “The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!” (Psalm 118:15). Then they say it again, and they add that the right hand of the LORD is exalted. The whole tent is cheering for what the LORD does.

The answer is False. The writer says, “The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death.” (Psalm 118:18). He doesn't hide the hard part, friends. He says it plainly, and he says what didn't happen too.

He wants to go in to give thanks to the LORD. He says, “Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD.” (Psalm 118:19). He wants through that gate so he can say thank you. Honestly, that's a better reason than most of mine for walking into a room.
The answer is False. The psalm says, “This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.” (Psalm 118:20). The priests aren't named there, friends. It's the righteous who enter.

The stone becomes the cornerstone. “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Psalm 118:22). The builders turned it down, and it ended up as the cornerstone. That's quite a turn for one stone, bakers.
The answer is True. The writer says, “This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Psalm 118:23). He says the LORD is behind it, friends. He also says it's marvelous in our eyes.

We will rejoice and be glad in it. “This is the day that the LORD has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.” (Psalm 118:24). The day is from the LORD, and the response is rejoicing. That's the kind of line you can say out loud before your alarm even goes off.

He asks the LORD to save us and cause us to prosper. The prayer says, “O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper!” (Psalm 118:25). Two requests, both short, both to the LORD. He asks plainly and doesn't dress it up.

The word is light. The psalm says, “The LORD is God; He has made His light to shine upon us.” (Psalm 118:27). I spent years in the dark of a junk drawer, friends, so I'll tell you light is a big deal. And this is the light He made to shine upon us.
